# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological innovations, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and subsequently drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. While DES dramatically reduced restenosis and target-lesion revascularization, the permanent metallic caging of the vessel raised concerns regarding chronic inflammation, impaired vasomotion, late stent thrombosis, and limitations for future revascularization [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) emerged as a conceptually attractive solution, intended to provide transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery before complete resorption, thereby restoring native vessel physiology [4].

## Concept and Device Design

The dominant clinical experience derives from the everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactide (PLLA) Absorb scaffold (Abbott Vascular) [5]. PLLA degrades via hydrolysis into lactic acid, ultimately metabolized through the Krebs cycle, with full resorption occurring over approximately two to three years [6]. The theoretical advantages included late lumen enlargement, recovery of vasomotor function, freedom from a permanent foreign body, and preservation of side-branch access [7]. Other devices, including magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris) and various polymeric platforms, were developed in parallel [8].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human ABSORB cohort A and B studies demonstrated feasibility, with serial imaging confirming scaffold resorption and partial restoration of vasoreactivity [9,10]. These encouraging findings catalyzed larger randomized trials. The ABSORB II trial compared the Absorb scaffold with the Xience metallic DES, but failed to demonstrate superior vasomotion and showed inferior late lumen dimensions [11]. ABSORB III, a pivotal trial supporting United States regulatory approval, reported non-inferiority for target-lesion failure at one year, though with a numerically higher rate of device thrombosis [12].

## Emerging Safety Concerns

As follow-up matured, accumulating data revealed an excess of scaffold thrombosis, particularly very late events occurring after one year [13,14]. Meta-analyses pooling randomized trials confirmed a significantly increased risk of device thrombosis with Absorb compared with everolimus-eluting metallic stents [15,16]. The longer-term follow-up of ABSORB II showed a disturbing signal of late events and no benefit in vasomotor reactivity [17]. Similarly, ABSORB III three-year outcomes demonstrated persistently higher target-lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis [18].

## Mechanistic Insights

Intravascular imaging studies clarified the mechanisms underlying these adverse outcomes. The relatively thick struts (≈150 µm) of the first-generation Absorb scaffold disrupted laminar flow, promoting thrombus formation [19]. Malapposition, incomplete lesion coverage, scaffold discontinuities during resorption, and uncovered struts were identified as substrates for late thrombotic events [20,21]. Suboptimal implantation technique—including inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and insufficient post-dilatation—was strongly implicated [22]. The "PSP" technique (adequate Preparation, appropriate Sizing, and high-pressure Post-dilatation) was subsequently advocated to improve outcomes [23].

## Regulatory and Clinical Decline

The convergence of unfavorable trial data and real-world registries led Abbott to withdraw the Absorb scaffold from commercial markets in 2017 [24]. Patient-level pooled analyses and network meta-analyses reinforced the unfavorable risk–benefit profile relative to contemporary thin-strut DES [25,26]. Nonetheless, longer-term follow-up suggested that the excess hazard might attenuate after complete resorption, with some studies indicating convergence of event curves beyond three years [27].

## Future Directions

The BVS experience has not extinguished interest in fully resorbable technology but has reframed development priorities [28]. Next-generation scaffolds aim for thinner struts, improved radial strength, faster and more predictable resorption, and enhanced deliverability [29]. Magnesium-based scaffolds and novel polymer platforms continue clinical evaluation, with refined implantation protocols and rigorous patient selection. The lessons of the first generation underscore that meticulous technique, appropriate lesion selection (avoiding small or heavily calcified vessels), and robust imaging guidance are essential prerequisites for any resorbable platform to succeed [30].

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented an elegant biological concept that ultimately failed to deliver the anticipated clinical advantages in their first iteration, owing to mechanical limitations and increased thrombotic risk. The rise and fall of the Absorb scaffold offers a cautionary lesson in device development, emphasizing the importance of strut thickness, implantation technique, and long-term randomized evidence. Whether refined next-generation devices can fulfil the original promise of "leaving nothing behind" remains an open and active question.
